How browser-side image compression works — and why it's different from server tools

Most image compressors online upload your file to a server, run compression on server hardware, then let you download the result. Aeroniqx's image compressor works differently: when you select an image, it's loaded into a browser Canvas element using the HTML5 Canvas API. The Canvas API's toBlob() method re-encodes the canvas at the JPEG quality level you specify. The entire operation happens in your browser's memory — the image never leaves your device. This is verifiable: open DevTools → Network tab while compressing, and you'll see zero requests containing your image data.

The trade-off is real: server-side compressors (like TinyPNG or Squoosh's server mode) can use more aggressive algorithms like MozJPEG, which applies additional optimisation passes after JPEG encoding to squeeze out another 5–15% compared to standard browser JPEG encoding. For most use cases — WhatsApp sharing, email attachments, government portal uploads — the difference is irrelevant. For professional web publishing where every KB matters, a tool like Squoosh with MozJPEG selected may produce slightly smaller files.

JPEG, PNG, WebP — which format to pick and when

JPEG is the right choice for photographs, product shots, and any image with continuous colour gradients. JPEG uses lossy compression that discards colour information the human eye doesn't easily detect. At quality 80%, a JPEG is typically 70–80% smaller than the same image as PNG, with no perceptible quality difference to most viewers. The limitation: JPEG doesn't support transparency. If you need a transparent background (logos, cutout product images), JPEG will add a white or coloured background instead.

PNG uses lossless compression — it reduces file size without discarding any image data. This makes PNG ideal for screenshots, graphics with text, logos, and images with flat colour areas. The "lossless" quality slider in this tool affects PNG by reducing the colour palette rather than discarding data — going below 70% on a complex photograph in PNG mode will make the file noticeably degraded. For photos, always use JPEG. For logos and screenshots, use PNG.

WebP is Google's image format — it supports both lossy (like JPEG) and lossless (like PNG) compression, typically producing 25–35% smaller files than JPEG at equivalent visual quality. WebP supports transparency and animation. The catch: older software doesn't support it. WhatsApp (as of 2024) accepts WebP on Android but not on all iOS versions. Word, older versions of Photoshop, and some government portal upload fields don't accept WebP. If you're compressing for a specific destination, check whether it accepts WebP before committing — JPEG is safer for portals, email, and document embeds.

The target file size feature — how the binary search works

When you enable "Target file size" and enter a value (say, 200 KB), the compressor doesn't just guess a quality setting — it runs a binary search. It starts at quality 50%, checks the resulting file size, then adjusts up or down based on whether the result was too large or too small, and repeats until the file is within a close margin of your target or it's exhausted the search range. This typically converges in 8–12 iterations (imperceptible, runs in under a second for most images).

This feature exists specifically because government and institutional portals in India have strict file size requirements: Passport Seva requires photos under 1 MB, UPSC application photos under 300 KB, JEE/NEET scanned documents under 100 KB, and most bank KYC portals accept images only up to 500 KB. Instead of guessing quality levels and re-compressing repeatedly, enter the portal's limit and the tool finds the right quality automatically.

The warning "Could not reach X KB" appears when the image content is too high-frequency (complex textures, fine detail) to compress to your target without exceeding JPEG's minimum quality floor. In this case, either resize the image to smaller dimensions first (fewer pixels = smaller file regardless of quality), or accept the minimum achievable size shown in the warning.

Resizing and aspect ratio — what actually happens

When you change the width or height with the aspect ratio lock on (🔗), the other dimension updates automatically to maintain the original proportions. With the lock off (🔓), you can set arbitrary dimensions — useful for cropping to a specific aspect ratio for social media posts, but be aware that unconstrained resizing stretches the image, not crops it. The compressor draws the original image onto a Canvas at the new dimensions using bilinear interpolation (the browser's default scaling algorithm), then re-encodes that canvas. This is not the same as a proper image resampler like Lanczos — for significant downscaling (e.g., 4000px → 400px), the quality is fine. For upscaling (making the image bigger), the result will look blurry because you're inventing pixels that don't exist in the original.

A common use case: you have a 3 MB DSLR photo at 4000×3000px and need it under 200 KB for a portal. Resize to 800×600px first (which alone may drop it to 400–600 KB depending on complexity), then apply quality 80% compression to reach ~150–200 KB. Combining resize + compression is almost always more effective than compression alone for large photographs.

WhatsApp image compression — what the app does and how to work around it

WhatsApp compresses images again when you send them, regardless of how compressed they already are. The effective quality ceiling for WhatsApp-sent images is roughly equivalent to JPEG quality 70–75% at a maximum dimension of around 1600px on the longest side. If you send a 4000×3000px original, WhatsApp will downsample it to ~1600px width and re-encode it at its own quality setting — the result is often 100–200 KB regardless of your original file size. This means pre-compressing before WhatsApp is mostly pointless for photos. The exception: documents sent as files (not photos) don't get recompressed — send image files as "Document" in WhatsApp to preserve quality, though the recipient sees a download link rather than an inline preview.

Frequently asked questions

Does compressing an already-compressed JPEG degrade quality further?

Yes — this is called generation loss. Every time a JPEG is re-encoded (even at high quality), the lossy compression discards slightly different information than the previous pass, and the degradation compounds. At quality 90%+, the difference is invisible to the naked eye for 1–2 generations. At quality 60–70%, you may start to see JPEG artefacts (blocky patterns, colour banding) emerging after 2–3 re-compressions of the same image. For this reason, whenever possible, keep the original uncompressed file (straight from camera, or exported from Photoshop without JPEG compression) and compress fresh each time rather than re-compressing a JPEG.

The compressed file is bigger than the original — why?

This typically happens when you compress a PNG to PNG at high quality, or when the original image was already heavily compressed (a low-quality JPEG). Browser Canvas re-encodes the image fresh — if the original JPEG was at quality 40% and you compress it at quality 85%, the new file will be larger because you're encoding at higher quality than the original. Set the quality lower than the original, or switch to JPEG format if you're currently outputting PNG for a photographic image.

Can I compress multiple images at once?

Currently, one image at a time. Batch compression (select 20 photos, get 20 compressed outputs) is on the roadmap. The current architecture processes images sequentially in a single canvas — batch mode requires either a queue system or Web Workers to avoid blocking the browser UI during processing. For now, if you need to batch-compress, tools like Squoosh CLI or ImageMagick run locally on your computer and can process hundreds of images in a single command.

Is there a file size limit?

No hard limit — the constraint is your device's available RAM. Loading a 20 MB RAW-converted JPEG into a browser canvas uses roughly 4× the file size in RAM (the uncompressed pixel data: width × height × 4 bytes per pixel). A 20 MP photo (5472×3648px) uses about 80 MB of RAM as a canvas. Modern phones have 6+ GB RAM, so even large photos work fine. If the tool crashes or hangs on a very large image, it's a browser memory limit — try reducing the dimensions first before compressing.
